scenes.narration: Sixty-six kilometres per second. That's how fast an Orionid meteor hits our sky. So how can a grain of sand light it up?

scenes.narration: Speed. At that speed the grain vaporises about a hundred kilometres up, and the air around it glows. That's the streak.

scenes.narration: Each October, Earth ploughs through the trail of dust left by Halley's Comet. The grains are tiny, about the size of a grain of sand.

scenes.speaker: Meera

scenes.narration: Halley gives us two showers a year, the Orionids now and the Eta Aquariids in May. It last passed in 1986 and returns in 2061.
scenes.image_prompt: Photo-real shot of Arjun, Indian man about 35, on a rooftop at night, explaining with a small hand gesture, calm expression, side angle, stars behind him
scenes.speaker: Arjun

scenes.narration: The dust it shed long ago still drifts along its orbit, so we cross it every year.
scenes.image_prompt: Photo-real telescope pointed at the night sky under a starfield, drifting dust particles glowing faintly in the dark
scenes.speaker: Arjun

scenes.narration: The peak was 21 October. Under ideal dark skies you'd see up to about twenty an hour.

scenes.narration: A bright moon washed out the evening, but it set before dawn and left a dark window.

scenes.narration: Rates fall off through November, so expect fewer, not zero. Try after moonset and before dawn, with a clear dark sky.
